clue.text: Used for making notes on riverside litter?

parts.note: a bank is the land at the edge of a river
litter is discarded rubbish such as paper

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what rubbish by the river might be good for.
explanation.walkthrough: The '?' flags that 'notes' means banknotes, not jottings: bank paper is the stock banknotes are printed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Bank paper is the special stock from which currency notes are printed.

clue.text: Battle honour: for judges

annotationWithheld.why: Battle honour for judges (5): BENCH = judges, but no parse of 'Battle honour' giving BENCH has been found

clue.text: Novel, inter-town races here?

parts.note: something novel is new
to inter is to bury, and Bury is also a Lancashire town

explanation.surface: A new contest between towns is held at this course.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town near Manchester; one word fits both 'inter' and 'town'.
explanation.definitionFit: Newbury in Berkshire has a well-known horse racecourse.

clue.text: "Left the warm —— of the cheerful day" (Gray)

definitions.text: "Left the warm —— of the cheerful day" (Gray)

parts.words: "Left the warm —— of the cheerful day" (Gray)
parts.note: a line from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, with one word missing

explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled from Gray's Elegy: 'Left the warm precincts of the cheerful day, / Nor cast one longing ling'ring look behind?'
explanation.definitionFit: Precincts are the bounds or enclosed surroundings of a place, here the warm confines of life.

clue.text: Royal priest recreated by R. Jones, Perth

indicators.note: recreated means made over again in another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Jones from Perth plays a priest-king in a revival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recreated' shuffles the letters of R JONES and PERTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Prester John was the legendary Christian priest-king of medieval tales, ruling somewhere in Asia or Africa.

clue.text: Epitaph to cause a tear

explanation.surface: Words on a gravestone make a mourner weep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tear' rhymes with 'pear', a rent in cloth, not a drop from the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Requiescat in pace is carved on tombs, and to rip is to tear or split.

clue.text: Rent a hammer

explanation.surface: Someone pays the rent with a tool, or rents one.
explanation.walkthrough: Gavel is an old word for rent or tribute paid to a lord, as in the Kentish land custom gavelkind.
explanation.definitionFit: Gavel was a feudal payment of tribute; it is also the mallet an auctioneer or chairman strikes.

clue.text: A lively dance, see, in space

indicators.note: the word for see goes inside the word for space

parts.note: a gap is a space
lo is an old word meaning see or look

explanation.surface: Someone spots a lively dance happening in an open area.
explanation.definitionFit: The galop is a fast nineteenth-century ballroom dance in two-four time.

clue.text: Observe, perhaps, in so many words

indicators.note: perhaps signals the word is one possible arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on something stated outright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges OBSERVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wordy means using a great many more words than needed.

clue.text: Macaulay's proof-corrector?

parts.note: Macaulay wrote the Lays of Ancient Rome, so someone checking proofs of his poems reads lays

explanation.surface: Who checked Lord Macaulay's printer's proofs?
explanation.walkthrough: A reader also means a proof-reader; the real answer is the church layman licensed to lead services.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is a layman licensed to conduct some church services; read literally, a person reading poems called lays.

clue.text: Butler's 24 anagram' came from this

parts.note: Samuel Butler named his utopian novel Erewhon by rearranging a word meaning 'in no place'

explanation.surface: Someone wonders where Samuel Butler got the title of his ideal-state novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 across is UTOPIAN, so Butler's 24 is his utopian satire Erewhon, whose title is the letters of this word shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Erewhon reworks the letters of the word for no place at all, which is also the sense of Greek utopia.

clue.text: Horse takes' theologian round Frankish quarter

indicators.note: the theologian's name is placed around the next piece, enclosing it

parts.note: William Paley was an eighteenth-century English theologian, author of Natural Theology

indicators.note: a quarter of an eight-letter word is its first two letters

explanation.surface: A churchman sets out on horseback around the Frankish part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' is only a link. The theologian is William Paley, whose Natural Theology was standard reading at Cambridge, and 'quarter' takes two of the eight letters of 'Frankish', from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A palfrey is a light saddle horse of the Middle Ages, ridden especially by ladies.

clue.text: The one o'clock nymph'? .

parts.note: a time stated as 'o'clock' names an hour
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A nymph who appears at one in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: One o'clock is the first hour, read here as HOUR I with the numeral after.
explanation.definitionFit: A houri is one of the beautiful maidens of the Muslim paradise, a kind of nymph.

clue.text: Fury-poetically it is' one -means of communication

parts.note: 'tis is the poetic contraction of it is
I is the Roman numeral for one
a telephone is a means of communication

explanation.surface: A furious remark that the phone is, in verse, one way to talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fury' with a capital is one of the three Furies of Greek myth, not rage.
explanation.definitionFit: Tisiphone, the avenger of murder, is one of the three Erinyes of Greek myth.

clue.text: Aid to cleanliness of oneself or one's footwear?

definitions.text: Aid to cleanliness of oneself or one's footwear?

parts.words: Aid to cleanliness of oneself or one's footwear?
parts.note: a tub for washing oneself, read playfully as a wash for one's indoor shoes

explanation.surface: Something that cleans either you or your shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: The real object is a bath shaped like a shoe, with a covered end; the question reads it as a bath for slippers.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipper bath is a bathtub with one end raised and covered, shaped like a shoe.

clue.text: Call for a boat

explanation.surface: Someone hails a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoy is a cry to attract attention, as in ahoy, and also a heavy coastal sailing barge.

clue.text: Tribunal shows what Jupiter paid to Juno

explanation.surface: A court case recalls how the king of the gods wooed his queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Jupiter wooed Juno from the heights of Olympus, so his courtship was conducted from on high.
explanation.definitionFit: England's senior civil court is a tribunal; Jupiter's lofty wooing of Juno was courtship from above.

clue.text: Strain in vehicle-turning is a knotty problem

indicators.note: the strain is placed inside the vehicle-turning pair

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
a bend is a turn in a road
to rick is to sprain or wrench a joint

explanation.surface: A driver hurts their back turning the car round and finds it troublesome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knotty problem' looks like a hard puzzle but means literally a knot.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrick bend is a sailor's knot for joining two heavy ropes, so literally a knotted matter.

clue.text: When not on hand they may go to people's heads

definitions.text: When not on hand they may go to people's heads

parts.words: When not on hand they may go to people's heads
parts.note: squares of cloth for the hand, once that word is dropped, become cloths worn on the head

explanation.surface: Like strong drink, these things may go to people's heads when not to hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Take 'hand' off the front of the cloths used for wiping noses and what is left is worn over the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Kerchiefs are cloths worn over the head; the hand variety goes in the pocket.

clue.text: Jumpy type, King George as bargain-hunter

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George
someone hunting bargains is a shopper

explanation.surface: A nervous king hunts for bargains.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect leaps about, so it is a jumping creature.

clue.text: Like a party-lover's confession

parts.note: a Conservative supporter admits membership in three words, which also run together as an adjective about love

explanation.surface: A partygoer admits to loving a good time.
explanation.walkthrough: The confession is 'I am a Tory', a lover of the Conservative party; run together it means loving.
explanation.definitionFit: Amatory means to do with sexual love, as love poetry or amorous behaviour.

clue.text: This head produces a report

parts.note: this word placed before 'head' makes an explosive missile tip, and a report is the bang of an explosion

explanation.surface: A head of department issues a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'report' means a loud bang, not a document; 'This' in front of 'head' makes the bomb part.
explanation.definitionFit: A warhead is the explosive tip of a missile, which goes off with a report.

clue.text: Like the wanted man on the mat.

explanation.surface: A wanted fugitive is caught in the doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanted man' suggests a fugitive, but means a guest whom people want; 'on the mat' is the word on a doormat.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest someone wants is gladly received, and that friendly greeting is printed on doormats.

clue.text: One who' could punish drink about ten?

indicators.note: the drink goes around the number, enclosing it

parts.note: a chaser is a drink taken after another, such as beer after spirits

explanation.surface: Someone might be punished for having a drink at about ten o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: To chasten is to discipline or punish, so this is someone who disciplines.

clue.text: "Drink not the —— glass" (Herbert)

parts.note: a line from George Herbert's poem The Church-Porch, warning against one drink too many, with one word missing

explanation.walkthrough: George Herbert's The Church-Porch: 'Drink not the third glass, which thou canst not tame.'
explanation.definitionFit: The glass after the second is the one in position number three in sequence.

clue.text: Grass loaf preferable 'to no…bread

explanation.surface: A loaf made of grass is better than going without.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb runs 'half a loaf is better than no bread', so the words before 'loaf' are the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Halfa is esparto, a North African grass; the proverb says a part of a loaf beats no bread at all.

clue.text: A male delegate?

parts.note: a gent is a man

explanation.surface: Asks whether the representative is a man.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent is a person who acts on another's behalf, a representative.

clue.text: Like'9's perfect state

parts.note: Thomas More's ideal commonwealth takes its Greek name from 'no place', the answer to 9 across

explanation.surface: Describing an ideal country that exists in no place.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 across is NOWHERE, and More's Utopia comes from Greek ou topos, 'no place'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas More's ideal island was named from Greek words for no place.

clue.text: Silent assent from, a retiring fellow'

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a don is a fellow of a college at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A shy academic agrees without saying a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dip of the head signals agreement without speech.

clue.text: Flower put, in phenomenally back to front

indicators.note: the letters found are then read in reverse order
the answer lies inside the single word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone puts a flower in, and it looks remarkably backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put' just links: ENOMENA sits inside 'phenomenally' and reads backwards as the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The anemone is a flowering plant of the buttercup family.

clue.text: Played to get the old copper:

parts.note: ye is an archaic spelling of the
D was the abbreviation for an old penny, a copper coin

explanation.surface: Someone played a game to win an old penny.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971, British pennies were written d (from Latin denarius) and were copper coins.
explanation.definitionFit: To toy with something is to play or trifle with it.

clue.text: Bursting at the seams? It's those odd inches, Ted!

indicators.note: odd suggests these letters are strange, set in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone tells Ted his trousers are splitting because of a few extra inches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges INCHES and TED.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanists call a seed pod or fruit dehiscent when it splits open along a line to release its seeds.
